title: Probability: ES failure as the event that a 'random' prime avoids infinitely many independent residue classes — a Borel–Cantelli on the covering classes
connection: If p's residues mod a (for a ≡ −1 mod 4C) were independent uniform, P(p avoids class r_{C,a} for all (C,a) ≤ K) = Π (1 − 1/a) ≈ exp(−Σ 1/a) → 0 as K → ∞ since Σ_{a ≡ −1 (4C)} 1/a diverges (like (1/φ(4C)) log). Borel–Cantelli direction 'infinitely many events occur a.s.' — the point is that for ONE p the events are deterministic, but the independence heuristic says failure is impossible; a rigorous version is the Kubilius model / Turán–Kubilius for 'residues of p across moduli'.
why: The Kubilius model gives rigorous approximation of arithmetic functions by independent random variables *on average over p*; its pointwise version is the Erdős–Kac-type concentration. Here we need 'for each p' — but a Turán–Kubilius variance bound over p ∈ [X, 2X] gives that the number of p ≤ X avoiding all classes ≤ K is ≪ X·exp(−c log K) + error; with K ≈ X^ε this is the Vaughan-type exceptional set bound by elementary means. Re-derive and compare constants.
first_step: Do the Turán–Kubilius-style second-moment calculation for the C-form classes; compare the resulting E(N) bound with Vaughan's; note any slack.

Compute the dependency structure: events E_{C,a} = {p ≡ r mod a} for different a are dependent only via CRT (independent for coprime moduli!).
why: Since residues mod coprime moduli are 'independent' in the CRT sense, the LLL/CRT construction shows there exist INTEGERS avoiding any finite collection of classes (as long as the classes don't cover) — but primality is the constraint that breaks the construction; so a counterexample must exist as an integer for each finite K (trivial: odd squares!) and ES hinges on primality + infinitely many K. Record precisely as a 'what the problem is' statement.

Write up the distinction and the role of primality in the C-form: p prime enters only via... nothing?! title: Proof of the isosceles law: x = y ⟺ (4x − 2p)(4z − p) = 2p²
connection: 2/x + 1/z = 4/p ⟺ (4x − 2p)(4z − p) = 2p², so A = 4x − 2p ∈ {2, 2p, 2p²} (≡ 2 mod 4) and B = 4z − p ∈ {p², p, 1} must be ≡ −p (mod 4): impossible iff p ≡ 1 (4). The shape y = z gives (4x − p)(4z − 2p) = 2p² with the same conclusion. Hence isosceles solutions exist ⟺ p ≢ 1 (mod 4) (p odd prime) — confirming the data exactly.
why: A complete, elementary proof of an empirical fingerprint: the degenerate (isosceles) locus of the ES surface is obstructed exactly on the hard class by a mod-4 divisor condition — a miniature T1-type reciprocity obstruction; for general n it predicts failure ⟺ every prime factor of n is ≡ 1 (mod 4) — verified exactly for all 2 ≤ n ≤ 3000 (344 numbers, = A004613 minus 1).

title: ES with large C (C up to p or p²): is the problem *easier* with a power-size reservoir, and does it still imply something?
connection: ES(p) only needs ONE C; nothing stops C from being huge. With C ≤ p^A the number of candidate C is p^A, the expected number of wins Σ_{C ≤ p^A} 1/φ(4C)·(…) ≈ A log p — still log! (Each C wins with probability ~1/φ(4C)... no wait: probability that 4Cp+1 has a divisor ≡ −1 mod 4C is roughly (number of divisors)/φ(4C) ≈ log(4Cp)/(4C)… so Σ_C log(Cp)/C ≈ log p · log X.) So count ≈ log p · log X even with X = p^A — logarithmic in X, confirming B3 for Type II. BUT in the e-slice/Type I forms, parameters (c, d) are two-dimensional: #(c,d) ≤ X² with win-probability 1/φ(4cd)·τ — Σ_{c,d ≤ X} τ(p² + 4c²d)/(4cd) ≈ log p · log²X. Still polylog. Confirms: no power reservoir in any parametrisation. Record as a calibration item.
why: Documents rigorously that every parametrisation has a polylog expected count regardless of the range; useful as a lemma for the 'generator matrix'.
first_step: Write the expected-count computation for Type I, Type II, and e-slice forms with ranges up to p^A; confirm polylog; check against ES_APPROACH_GENERATORS §B3.

title: Experimental: do certificates for p and for p' = p + 4Ck share structure when 4Cp+1 and 4Cp'+1 share factors?
connection: 4Cp' + 1 = 4Cp + 1 + 16C²k; sharing a divisor a requires 16C²k ≡ 0 mod a. So certificates with divisor a propagate along p ≡ p₀ (mod a) — the covering class. This is the 'template reuse' structure; the experiment is to measure how far a single template's class extends (its density of primes actually certified = 1/a · (all primes in the class) — trivially all? YES: if a | 4Cp+1 and a ≡ −1 mod 4C then for every p' ≡ p mod a, a | 4Cp'+1 too, and the cofactor b' = (4Cp'+1)/a ≡ ? mod 4C: 4Cp'+1 ≡ 1 mod 4C, a ≡ −1 ⟹ b' ≡ −1 ✓.) So each (C, a) certifies the entire class p ≡ −(4C)^{−1} mod a. Record as a lemma.
why: This is exactly the covering-system structure of the C-form: each certificate is a residue class of modulus a ≡ −1 (mod 4C). ES (C-form part) ⟺ primes ⊂ ∪ classes. Make the lemma explicit; cross-check with the exceptional primes 409 etc. (they lie in no class with a ≤ 6000 or so).

title: Analogy: Lehmer's totient problem / 'Giuga numbers' — sets defined by 'all prime factors satisfy a congruence' are provably thin and structured; the C-form failure set is such a set for each C
connection: For C = 1: 4p + 1 ∈ S₁ := {all prime factors ≡ 1 mod 4} — the 'sum of two squares' type set. For general C: 4Cp+1 ∈ S_C := {subset products of prime factors avoid −1 mod 4C}. Each S_C is a 'multiplicatively defined' set with a Landau-type counting function x/(log x)^{1−δ_C}; the failure set is {p : ∀C, 4Cp + 1 ∈ S_C}. Sets of the form {n : ∀C ≤ K, aC n + b ∈ S_C} are 'simultaneous Landau conditions on linear forms' — a sieve-theoretic object with a known theory for FIXED K (Brun–Hooley), and the uniformity in K is the frontier.

title: Erdős–Faber–Lovász: absorption for a universal finite coloring bound
connection: EFL shares F01, F05w, F23: a universal finite-structure assertion proved (Kang–Kelly–Kühn–Methuku–Osthus, arXiv:2101.04698) for all sufficiently large n; small n are not covered by that proof. Its absorption proof is a candidate pattern for ES's infinite family of thin certificate lines (F34).
why: Absorption organizes many near-solutions into a small reservoir that completes arbitrary leftover structure; an arithmetic analogue might patch uncovered residue classes or prime families.
first_step: Read the proof’s absorption section and formulate an explicit ES analogue: a reservoir of certificate lines that absorbs a bounded set of uncovered prime residue patterns.

title: Addition chains feature flip: minimization versus mere existence
connection: Scholz–Brauer shares ES’s universal integers, short word certificates, and constructive recurrences (F01,F16w,F32), but asks for a near-optimal shortest chain rather than any witness. The flipped optimality constraint is what creates its sharp lower-bound difficulty.
why: It separates certificate existence from minimization, cautioning against importing optimization barriers into ES’s pure existence problem.
first_step: Compare the proof’s chain-length inequalities with ES parameter-size bounds and discard any step that depends on optimality.

title: Markov uniqueness feature flip: uniqueness of maximal coordinate
connection: The Markov uniqueness conjecture shares ES’s cubic integral points, coordinate symmetry, and Vieta-type involutions (F13,F14,F38), but asks uniqueness of a maximal coordinate rather than existence. This feature flip spotlights orbit collisions, not missing witnesses.
why: If ES has many witnesses, Markov-style uniqueness machinery is not directly useful; however its canonical-representative methods may simplify counts.
first_step: Read the uniqueness conjecture statement and compare its mutation-tree fundamental domain with ES’s S₃-reduced solution count.

title: Frobenius problem feature flip: fixed embedding dimension
connection: Three-generator semigroups share ES’s universal integer parameter, divisibility certificates, and finite exception analysis (F01,F10,F25), but the Frobenius number is an output of chosen generators, not a witness for each input. This flip highlights the direction of quantifiers.
why: Quantifier reversal suggests avoiding semigroup results that only classify outputs; useful transfer is the residue enumeration, not the theorem’s existence conclusion.
first_step: Write the exact ∀generators ∃largest-gap quantifiers beside ES’s ∀n∃triple, then identify which Apéry formulas preserve the latter direction.

title: Erdős–Faber–Lovász feature flip: exact bound versus asymptotic bound
connection: EFL shares ES’s universal finite objects, covering structure, and computational finite verification (F01,F03,F23), but an asymptotic ‘large n’ theorem alone does not cover small instances. ES likewise needs all n, not almost all.
why: The large-instance/small-exception split offers a proof organization for ES: analytic range plus explicit finite verification, provided the analytic threshold is reachable.
first_step: Extract the large-n threshold from the EFL proof and compare the role of finite verification with ES’s computational range.

title: Addition-chain certificate-size analogy for ES witnesses
connection: Addition chains and ES share F01,F23,F24,F32: universal arithmetic targets, finite certificates, computational checking, and heuristic expectations of manageable witness size. ES denominators can be checked exactly in polynomial-time arithmetic.
why: Certificate complexity framing may yield a clean fixed-parameter search and distinguish search difficulty from witness-verification difficulty.
first_step: Bound the bit-length of ES witness coordinates in terms of p for each known parametrized family and compare with generic addition-chain length bounds.

title: Four-unit-fraction representations
connection: The four-term Egyptian fraction problem shares F01, F12, F27, F33, while adding a spare summand changes the geometry of the equation.
why: Determine whether a controlled four-term identity can be compressed to three terms using a divisor condition.
first_step: Classify standard four-term constructions by whether two terms combine to a unit fraction and test the resulting divisibility condition for p.

title: Sums of two unit fractions and multiplication tables
connection: Two-term reciprocal equations share F10, F15, F33 and reduce to factor pairs, much like each fixed-x ES fibre.
why: The elementary factor-pair analysis supplies exact interval and congruence controls for ES slices.
first_step: Write the two-term equation as (a y−b)(a z−b)=c and catalogue the bounds retained when one term is fixed.

title: Function-field Egyptian fractions
connection: Function-field analogues share F01, F12, F26, F27 and replace integer primes by irreducible polynomials.
why: The proof may reveal which steps rely on archimedean size versus factorisation and congruences.
first_step: Locate the function-field ES proof and translate its key divisor-counting lemma to integer primes, marking the exact failed estimate.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Unit-fraction equations over polynomial rings
connection: Polynomial-ring reciprocal equations share F12, F13, F26 and often admit algebraic factorisation unavailable over integers.
why: Factorisation patterns can suggest new identities or show why integer size is the obstruction.
first_step: Compare the polynomial proof's factorisation with the integer identity (4x−p)(4y−p)(4z−p) variants.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Infinite covering systems by parametrised families
connection: Infinite covering problems share F03w, F30, F34 and replace one finite certificate with infinitely many thin families.
why: A structured infinite cover could accommodate the square-class failures of current finite templates.
first_step: Sort known ES families by prime density and overlap; formulate a criterion under which their union covers all primes.

title: Finite certificate impossibility and polynomial values
connection: Bounded-certificate failures share F09, F35, F36 and show that fixed algebraic templates can miss infinitely many inputs.
why: The obstruction can help identify what additional parameter dependence a successful ES argument must exploit.
first_step: Read the proof of the conditional no-finite-scheme result and list precisely which assumptions fail for infinite or adaptive schemes.

title: Formal verification of exhaustive congruence arguments
connection: Finite congruence proofs share F03, F23, F32 and can be checked by small proof certificates.
why: A machine-checked database of identities could safely expand the current congruence toolkit and detect missed classes.
first_step: Encode the standard ES Mordell identities and their residue coverage in a proof assistant or a short independently audited checker.

title: Feature flip F18: SL₂(ℤ) → SL₂(ℤ[i]) / Bianchi groups — Gaussian words for p ≡ 1 mod 4
connection: ES's SL₂ form asks for [[a,p],[c,d]] with congruence conditions. Over ℤ[i], p = ππ̄ splits; a Gaussian SL₂ version could split the problem into two conjugate halves.
why: Hard primes split in ℤ[i] (F29); a formulation where the splitting is visible could separate T1-type obstructions (which concern rational squares) from the generic case.
first_step: Write the SL₂(ℤ[i]) analogue with entry π and conditions mod (1+i)^k c; check whether norm maps produce ES matrices.

title: Feature flip F28: Type III-like solutions for composite n (neither type, e.g. 4/9 = 1/4 + 1/6 + 1/36) — the T1-free channel at squares
connection: For n = m², Type I/II vanish (T1) but ES(m²) holds via solutions not of Type I/II (e.g. 4/9 = 1/4 + 1/6 + 1/36). Mixed-type solutions are the channel T1 does not see.
why: Understanding how ES survives at squares (via factor m) clarifies why primes cannot use that channel and what a 'prime analogue' would be.
first_step: Classify all ES solutions of 4/m² for odd m ≤ 101 by gcd pattern with m; check whether every one is a scaled solution of 4/d for d | m, d < m².

title: Erdős reciprocal-sum conjecture (OAI 159, claimed) applied to the failure set
connection: OAI 159 claims every set with divergent reciprocal sum contains arbitrarily long APs; the ES failure set E ⊂ primes has convergent reciprocal sum already (Vaughan), so the theorem gives no constraint — a calibration that the failure set is too sparse for density Ramsey theory.
why: Records a negative transfer explicitly so later lanes don't repeat it; also suggests which sparser Ramsey statements (for primes with Σ1/p convergent) would be needed.
first_step: Verify Σ_{p∈E} 1/p < ∞ from the repo's E(N) bound and note the threshold density for Green–Tao-type relative results.

title: Fermat two-squares via Thue's lemma (pigeonhole) as a template for ES at primes ≡ 1 (4)
connection: Thue: given ρ² ≡ −1 mod p, pigeonhole gives x ≡ ρy with |x|,|y| < √p, hence p = x² + y². ES's lattice L_ρ(g) uses ρ² ≡ −p mod g, a Thue-type lattice; certificates are short vectors with extra divisibility.
why: It is the most elementary pointwise prime theorem from a thick object (lattice of covolume p). ES needs the short vector to hit a divisor condition, which is where pigeonhole breaks.
first_step: Formulate the ES lattice-point condition as 'a short vector of L_ρ(g) lies in a sublattice of index k' and compute the pigeonhole threshold vs the actual vector lengths.

title: Erdős–Straus as a 'Conway's 99-graph'-style existence problem? — calibrating against open existence problems
connection: Not a translation but a calibration: ES has the profile 'finite check per instance, unbounded family, no structure forcing existence', shared by problems like the existence of certain strongly regular graphs or covering systems with odd moduli. Methods that settled such problems (e.g. the BBMST distortion method for Erdős–Selfridge) are relevant only when a structure theorem exists.
why: It records the meta-observation that ES belongs to the class where solutions came from either explicit constructions or global counting with exact structure.
first_step: List 5 solved 'every instance has a witness, witnesses are sparse' problems and the proof engine of each (overlaps with ES_APPROACH_GENERATORS G1).

title: Lehmer's τ(p) ≠ 0 as a structural twin of ES
connection: τ(p) ≠ 0 is open for every p although density-one non-vanishing is known and congruences (mod 691, 2^k, 3^k, 5, 7, 23) exclude vanishing on all but a thin set of residue classes. ES: Mordell identities exclude all but six classes mod 840; the remaining classes need size/structure input. Compare the two endgames.
why: Two famous 'non-vanishing at every prime' problems with identical architecture (congruence exclusion + thin residual set) — methods for one may inspire the other.
first_step: Write the comparison: what is known about the residual set for τ (e.g. τ(p) = 0 forces p in specific classes mod large M) vs ES's square classes; check whether ES has analogues of the mod-ℓ Galois-image arguments.

title: Box principle for windows: two windows with the same residue data combine
connection: Thue's lemma is a box principle. Pigeonhole windows e by the residue vector of p modulo small primes and the factorisation shape of N_e; two windows with equal data might combine (via CRT) into a certificate at the window e·e′ or at lcm, if a combination law exists.
why: Pigeonhole needs a combination law; windows have CRT structure that may supply one.
first_step: Test on data: for pairs of failing windows e, e′ with compatible data, check whether e·e′ (or another derived window) succeeds more often than random.
